**(The Frisky) —** Everybody has a “type.” Personally, I like a man with a big schnozz—bonus points if he has a collection of acne scars à la Tommy Lee Jones.

The “OverEater” is one of nine types of men women should avoid. My pal Annie likes preppy men—but only after they’ve gone to seed and become a little bloated in the process. Suzanne has a weakness for thin Japanese guys who like indie rock, while Maddy adores bike messengers of all shapes and sizes.

But certain types of guys should be nobody’s type. These men are distinguished by one thing: an overabundance of one or more very bad qualities. Here’s your guide to the boys to avoid:

**1. The OverSharer:** The current poster boy for oversharing is Phillip Nobel, who wrote a highly hide-chapping account of his extramarital affair for *Elle*. The OverSharer will broadcast intimate episodes from your relationship to his mother, your mother, his blog readers, and anyone else he can rope into paying attention.

**2. The OverThinker:** One of the great things about dating men is that you aren’t subjected to long, excruciating interrogations about what you really meant when you reassured him that, no, he didn’t look fat in those pants. However, though they’re rare birds, some guys will want to spend hours dissecting even the most innocuous comment, examining its tone, content, and what you might have been implying.

**3. The OverTalker:** Your friends say they’ve never known you to be so quiet. That’s because this man does enough talking for both of you—and then some. When you finally manage to eke out a sentence or two, he interrupts and talks over you anyway. You have two choices: accept that you will never speak again, or tell him goodbye. Your call.

**4. The OverDresser:** This dandy makes *Gossip Girl*’s Chuck Bass look sloppy and mismatched. The fact that he takes longer than you to get ready is strike one against him, but matching his socks to his underwear—and his ascot—drives him out of the park.

**5. The OverEater:** It’s an irritating fact that men can eat more than women. The OverEater doesn’t care. Food is his first love, and he’ll push cannoli and baked ziti on you like a crazed Italian granny. Unless you don’t mind a future spent in stretch pants, you might want to give this dude a pass.

**6. The OverReactor:** Remember when Russell Crowe threw a phone at the hotel clerk who somehow displeased him? That’s this guy. From the old lady who accidentally bumps into him at the grocery store to the SUV that cuts him off on the highway, everyone in his path will feel his wrath—you most of all. Do not walk away; run.

**7. The Over-the-Topper:** He’s the life of the party and thinks nothing of driving his motorcycle through the bar if he believes it will get a laugh. He’s certainly cute, but he never stops. He’s always on—and that will quickly become a turnoff.

**8. The OverAchiever:** Picture the male version of Tracy Flick from the movie *Election*, wearing perfectly fitted jeans and a crisp white Oxford shirt, with a copy of his—naturally perfect—SAT scores in his wallet. Now imagine making love to him. You can’t, can you?

**9. The OverCompensator:** Maybe he was the homeliest kid in his eighth-grade class, but that doesn’t mean you need to sit through a monologue about how much money he makes, how jealous his friends are of his new BMW, and how he could totally date supermodels if he wanted to. Next!

**(The Frisky)** — Most people are attracted to a particular kind of person. My own preference is for men with prominent noses, with extra credit for Tommy Lee Jones–style acne scarring. The “OverEater,” however, belongs to a list of nine male personalities women would be wise to steer clear of.

My friend Annie favors clean-cut, preppy men—but only once age has softened them and added a little puffiness. Suzanne is drawn to slender Japanese men who listen to indie rock, while Maddy loves bicycle couriers regardless of their build. Yet some men should appeal to no one at all. What sets them apart is an excessive amount of at least one deeply undesirable trait. Consider this a field guide to the men best avoided:

1. **The OverSharer:** Phillip Nobel currently serves as the prime example, thanks to the painfully irritating account of his affair that he wrote for *Elle*. A man like this will reveal private details about your relationship to his mother, your mother, his blog audience, and anyone else he can persuade to listen.

2. **The OverThinker:** One advantage of dating men is usually avoiding drawn-out questioning about what you actually meant when you told him that, no, those trousers did not make him look heavy. A few men are exceptions, though. They will devote hours to analyzing a harmless remark, scrutinizing its wording, delivery, and every possible hidden message.

3. **The OverTalker:** Your friends notice that you have become unusually silent, largely because he supplies more than enough conversation for both of you. If you manage to get a few words in, he cuts you off and keeps going. You can either resign yourself to never talking again or end the relationship. The decision is yours.

4. **The OverDresser:** Compared with this fashion-obsessed peacock, Chuck Bass from *Gossip Girl* appears carelessly dressed. Taking more time than you to prepare is already a mark against him. Coordinating his socks with both his underwear and his ascot goes far beyond that.

5. **The OverEater:** Annoyingly, men are generally able to consume more food than women. This fellow takes that difference to an extreme. Eating is his greatest passion, and he will press cannoli and baked ziti on you with the determination of an unhinged Italian grandmother. Unless a lifetime in elastic-waist clothing sounds appealing, consider skipping him.

6. **The OverReactor:** Think of Russell Crowe hurling a telephone at a hotel employee who had angered him. That is the model for this man. Whether it is an elderly woman who bumps into him by mistake at the supermarket or an SUV that cuts him off in traffic, anyone who crosses his path becomes a target for his fury—and you will receive more of it than anyone. Do not merely leave; get away fast.

7. **The Over-the-Topper:** He dominates every social gathering and would happily ride his motorcycle through a bar if he believed people would laugh. He may be attractive, but he never tones himself down. His constant performance quickly stops being charming.

8. **The OverAchiever:** Imagine a male Tracy Flick from the film *Election*, wearing impeccably tailored jeans and a spotless white Oxford shirt, with a copy of his predictably flawless SAT results tucked into his wallet. Then try to picture sleeping with him. Difficult, isn’t it?

9. **The OverCompensator:** Perhaps he was the least attractive boy in his eighth-grade class, but that does not obligate you to endure a speech about his salary, his friends’ envy of his new BMW, or his claim that he could date supermodels whenever he wished. Move along.

**TM & © 2008 TMV, Inc. | All Rights Reserved.**
outputs.L3:
Everyone has a preferred romantic “type,” whether that means someone adventurous, intellectual, funny, or affectionate. However, some men display negative qualities so excessively that dating them can become frustrating and emotionally draining. While everyone has flaws, certain habits may signal that a relationship will require more patience than it is worth.

The **OverSharer** has little sense of privacy. He publicizes intimate details about his relationship to family members, friends, blog readers, social media followers, and virtually anyone else willing to listen. Personal disagreements, private conversations, and romantic moments quickly become public knowledge. As a result, his partner may feel exposed and unable to trust him with sensitive information.

The **OverThinker** treats every harmless remark as though it contains a hidden message. He obsessively analyzes word choice, tone of voice, facial expressions, and possible implications. An ordinary comment can lead to repeated questions and lengthy discussions about what was “really” meant. Instead of allowing communication to remain natural, he creates tension by searching for problems that may not exist.

The **OverTalker** dominates almost every conversation. He interrupts frequently, tells long stories, and redirects discussions back to himself. His partner may struggle to finish a sentence or express an opinion before he takes control again. Over time, this behavior can make the relationship feel one-sided, as meaningful communication requires both people to listen as well as speak.

Finally, the **OverDresser** is excessively preoccupied with his appearance. He may spend an unreasonable amount of time getting ready, carefully coordinating every piece of clothing and obsessing over minor details. Taking pride in one’s appearance is generally positive, but excessive concern with fashion can become inconvenient—especially when it causes delays or makes appearance seem more important than the experience itself.

These traits may appear amusing at first, but in extreme forms they can undermine privacy, trust, communication, and mutual respect. A successful relationship depends not on finding someone without flaws, but on choosing a partner whose habits leave room for both people to feel heard, comfortable, and valued.

Dating often involves looking beyond first impressions and noticing behaviors that may become unhealthy over time. Some habits are merely quirks, but others reveal a lack of boundaries, balance, or consideration. A humorous way to recognize these warning signs is to sort them into exaggerated “types” of men best avoided.

The **OverSharer**, for example, treats private information as public property. He may reveal intimate details about past relationships, repeat personal stories told in confidence, or post every moment of his life online. His openness can initially seem refreshing, but it may soon become clear that he does not respect privacy—his own or anyone else’s.

The **OverThinker** turns every interaction into a puzzle. A delayed reply, an ordinary comment, or a minor change in tone can lead to endless questions and imagined explanations. Thoughtfulness is valuable, but constant analysis can create unnecessary tension and make a relationship feel exhausting.

Then there is the **OverTalker**, who dominates every conversation. He interrupts, redirects discussions toward himself, and rarely shows genuine curiosity about his date. Rather than creating a mutual exchange, he treats the other person as an audience. Over time, this behavior may signal self-absorption or an inability to listen.

The **OverDresser** is excessively preoccupied with appearance. Taking pride in personal style is not a problem, but an obsession with clothes, grooming, labels, or looking perfect can suggest vanity and misplaced priorities. If every outing revolves around his image, there may be little room left for spontaneity or emotional connection.

The point is not that talkative, thoughtful, stylish, or emotionally open men should automatically be rejected. The warning lies in the word “over.” When a trait becomes so excessive that it violates privacy, creates anxiety, silences a partner, or places appearance above substance, it can undermine a healthy relationship. Recognizing these patterns early can save time and frustration—and may be a good reason to move on.

# 9 Types of Men Women Should Avoid

Dating is a lot like shopping at a discount furniture warehouse: everything looks promising under fluorescent lighting, but some items are missing crucial screws. Before you invest six months and a shared streaming password, watch out for these nine romantic red flags in human form.

## 1. The OverSharer

You’ve barely taken a sip of your cocktail, and you already know about his parents’ divorce, his suspicious mole, and what his ex called him during their final couples-therapy session.

Emotional openness is great. Handing you the unabridged audiobook of his trauma before appetizers is not. If the first date feels like you should be billing his insurance, quietly request the check.

**Classic line:** “I don’t usually tell people this, but…”

## 2. The OverThinker

You text, “Had fun tonight!” He spends four hours analyzing whether the exclamation point indicates enthusiasm, sarcasm, or unresolved hostility.

The OverThinker cannot simply choose a restaurant. He must compare menus, parking options, online reviews, table acoustics, and the geopolitical implications of ordering tapas. By the time he decides, the restaurant has closed—and possibly been converted into luxury condos.

**Classic line:** “What did you mean by ‘sure’?”

## 3. The OverTalker

He doesn’t have conversations; he hosts a podcast you never subscribed to.

Ask him what he does for work, and 45 minutes later he’s explaining blockchain, his high-school football injury, and why *The Godfather Part III* is “actually misunderstood.” Your role is to nod occasionally and avoid dying of dehydration.

**Classic line:** “Sorry, I interrupted you. Anyway…”

## 4. The OverEater

This isn’t about appetite or body size. It’s about the man who orders “for the table,” eats 83 percent of it, steals your fries, and then asks whether you’re “really going to finish that.”

He treats every meal like a competitive event and your plate like disputed territory. One day it’s your mozzarella sticks. Next, it’s your hopes and dreams.

**Classic line:** “You weren’t eating those, were you?”

## 5. The Human Résumé

Within seven minutes, you know his job title, salary bracket, marathon time, credit score, and the fact that he once stood near a famous person at an airport.

He isn’t flirting; he’s pitching investors. The Human Résumé believes romance begins when you’re sufficiently impressed by his premium travel status.

**Classic line:** “Not to brag, but…”  
*Spoiler: He is absolutely about to brag.*

## 6. The Perpetual Victim

Every ex was “crazy.” Every boss was jealous. Every roommate betrayed him. Even the barista is apparently engaged in a long-term campaign to ruin his life via incorrect milk.

If every story ends with him as the blameless hero surrounded by villains, congratulations: you’ve met the common denominator.

**Classic line:** “Drama just follows me.”

## 7. The Future Faker

On date two, he’s naming your hypothetical children. By date four, he’s discussing a cottage in Vermont. By date six, he has vanished into the mist like a Victorian ghost with commitment issues.

The Future Faker loves the fantasy of intimacy, especially when it requires no present-day accountability.

**Classic line:** “When we go to Italy next summer…”

## 8. The Low-Effort Prince

His idea of making plans is texting “wyd” at 10:47 p.m. He considers putting on clean sweatpants a grand romantic gesture and expects applause for remembering your birthday month.

He isn’t “chill.” He is outsourcing the entire relationship to you.

**Classic line:** “I’m down for whatever.”  
**Translation:** “Please plan, reserve, remind, drive, and emotionally sustain everything.”

## 9. The Boundary Negotiator

You say you don’t want another drink; he orders one anyway. You say you need a night alone; he appears at your door with “a surprise.” You say no; he hears “begin persuasive closing argument.”

A decent partner respects boundaries the first time. He does not treat them like the terms-and-conditions box everyone clicks without reading.

**Classic line:** “Come on, don’t be like that.”

Ultimately, nobody is perfect. We all overshare, overthink, overtalk, or eat the last dumpling occasionally. The issue is not one awkward date—it’s the pattern. Look for someone who listens, respects you, takes responsibility, and leaves at least one mozzarella stick.

That, friends, is romance.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

# Your Romantic “Type” Is Real—and It May Be Ruining Your Life

Everyone has a type. Maybe yours is tall, dark, and emotionally unavailable. Maybe it’s “creative,” which somehow always means unemployed but very intense about vinyl. Maybe it’s men who own exactly one towel and insist they’re “low-maintenance.”

Attraction is mysterious, powerful, and occasionally in need of adult supervision. So before chemistry persuades you that another human warning label is actually “intriguing,” familiarize yourself with these nine personality types best admired from a safe distance—preferably through binoculars, from another postcode.

### 1. The Human Podcast

He doesn’t converse; he broadcasts. Every discussion becomes a four-part series called *His Thoughts*, with no guest speakers and absolutely no listener questions. Mention your promotion, and he’ll explain ambition to you. Mention your dog, and he’ll recount every pet he has ever met. His favorite phrase is “To play devil’s advocate,” because apparently Satan needed an unpaid intern.

### 2. The Perpetual Victim

Every ex was “crazy.” Every boss was “threatened by him.” Every roommate was unreasonable about rent, dishes, and indoor fireworks. Nothing is ever his fault—not even the things you watched him do while making direct eye contact. Dating him means becoming the newest character in an ongoing conspiracy against one innocent man who simply cannot catch a break or apologize.

### 3. The Future-Faker

By date two, he’s planning your Tuscan wedding, naming your children, and researching a “little place” in Lisbon. By week three, he needs space because things are “moving too fast.” Sir, you were the one pricing villas. He sells emotional timeshares: dazzling presentation, complimentary champagne, and absolutely no property at the end.

### 4. The Bare-Minimum Visionary

He wants applause for texting back before sunrise, remembering your surname, or placing a plate near the dishwasher. Ask for emotional support and he’ll stare as if you’ve requested a kidney in a decorative gift box. His romantic philosophy is simple: if the bar is on the floor, bring a shovel.

### 5. The Personal-Development Peacock

His bookshelf is full of habit manuals, leadership manifestos, and one pristine journal labeled *GRIND*. He wakes at 4:45 a.m. to optimize his mitochondria but somehow can’t schedule a dentist appointment. Every relationship problem is an “opportunity for growth”—specifically yours. He isn’t avoiding accountability; he’s “protecting his energy.”

### 6. The Jealous Detective

He notices who liked your photo, why you took seven minutes to reply, and whether the waiter’s “Enjoy your meal” sounded suspiciously intimate. He calls it protectiveness; the rest of civilization calls it exhausting. A partner should not require you to submit a quarterly report on your eye contact with male baristas.

### 7. The Weaponized-Incompetence Wizard

He “doesn’t know how” to buy groceries, fold laundry, book a table, or locate the bin while standing beside it. Yet he can assemble a gaming computer from loose wires and rage. This is not helplessness. It is strategic confusion, performed in the hope that you’ll become his girlfriend, mother, secretary, and unpaid household operations manager.

### 8. The Too-Cool-to-Care Cynic

He mocks enthusiasm because having interests might expose him to joy. Your favorite show is basic, weddings are cringe, birthdays are capitalist propaganda, and sincerity gives him hives. He thinks detachment makes him mysterious. Mostly, it makes dinner feel like you’ve been seated beside a damp review section.

### 9. The Commitment Escape Artist

He wants intimacy without labels, loyalty without responsibility, and all your weekends without appearing in a single photograph. After eighteen months, he’s still “seeing where this goes,” apparently awaiting geological confirmation. He’ll insist labels don’t matter—right up until you label him “single,” at which point he discovers a passionate interest in definitions.

Having a type isn’t the problem. Repeatedly choosing the same red flag in different trousers is. Chemistry may start the engine, but character determines whether the car reaches a pleasant destination or leaves you crying beside a motorway while he says he’s “not great with conflict.”

Choose accordingly.

# Dating the “Overs”: 9 Big Personalities and How to Keep Your Cool

Dating is already a lot. Dating someone who does *everything* at maximum volume? That can be hilarious, exhausting—and surprisingly charming. Here’s your playful field guide to navigating nine classic “Overs.”

## 1. The OverSharer  
By the appetizers, you know their childhood nickname, credit score, and cousin’s ongoing divorce drama.

**Dating advice:** Appreciate the openness, but set a comfortable pace. Try: “I like getting to know you—let’s save a few plot twists for date three.”

**Hidden upside:** You’ll never spend six months wondering what they’re feeling.

---

## 2. The OverThinker  
Your period instead of an exclamation point has launched a full internal investigation.

**Dating advice:** Communicate clearly and consistently. Reassurance helps, but don’t become a 24/7 interpretation service. Encourage them to ask rather than analyze.

**Hidden upside:** They’ve already considered every possible vacation itinerary—and packed backup chargers.

---

## 3. The OverTalker  
You asked how their day was. Forty-seven minutes later, they’re explaining a coworker’s sourdough starter.

**Dating advice:** Interrupt kindly and make conversation-sharing explicit: “Pause—I want to jump in before I forget.” A good date should be tennis, not a podcast.

**Hidden upside:** Awkward silences have been permanently canceled.

---

## 4. The OverDresser  
You suggested “casual drinks.” They arrived looking ready to accept an international film award.

**Dating advice:** Let them sparkle. If the dress code matters, be specific: “Sneakers-and-jeans casual, outdoor picnic, possibly muddy.”

**Hidden upside:** Your couple photos will look expensive.

---

## 5. The OverEater  
They ordered one of everything “for the table,” and apparently *they are the table*.

**Dating advice:** Skip judgment and focus on compatibility. Share dishes, discuss budgets if necessary, and don’t police another adult’s plate.

**Hidden upside:** They’ll know every great restaurant—and dessert is never an afterthought.

---

## 6. The OverReactor  
The restaurant lost your reservation, so naturally civilization has collapsed.

**Dating advice:** Stay calm without dismissing their feelings. Validate first—“Yeah, that’s frustrating”—then move toward solutions. If explosive reactions become frequent or cruel, set firm boundaries.

**Hidden upside:** Good news receives a standing ovation.

---

## 7. The Over-The-Topper  
A one-month anniversary somehow involves fireworks, a string quartet, and a customized weather balloon.

**Dating advice:** Enjoy the spectacle, but clarify that affection doesn’t need a production budget. Suggest small gestures that still feel meaningful.

**Hidden upside:** You will never receive a birthday card that merely says “Happy Birthday.”

---

## 8. The OverAchiever  
They’ve finished a workout, answered 32 emails, and learned conversational Italian before you’ve found your socks.

**Dating advice:** Don’t compete. Celebrate their ambition while protecting time for rest, play, and connection. Romance should not become another performance metric.

**Hidden upside:** Reservations are booked, plans are confirmed, and the shared calendar is color-coded.

---

## 9. The OverCompensator  
They missed one text, so they sent flowers, a handwritten apology, and possibly a small parade.

**Dating advice:** Reassure them that ordinary mistakes don’t require grand restitution. Encourage direct apologies, changed behavior, and proportionate gestures.

**Hidden upside:** They care deeply—sometimes with overnight shipping.

---

## The Bottom Line

Most “Over” traits are strengths with the volume turned up: honesty, thoughtfulness, enthusiasm, appetite, ambition, generosity. The goal isn’t to turn someone down to zero. It’s to find a volume you can both enjoy—and to know when a quirky habit crosses into disrespect, control, or incompatibility.

After all, the right person may be “too much” for someone else—and exactly enough for you.
